opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to notice is that $100 billion a year sounds like a big number, and in absolute terms it is. It would make OpenAI one of the larger companies in the world by revenue. But if you put it in the context of the overall economy, it's actually quite modest. World GDP is somewhere around $100 trillion a year, so we're talking about roughly a tenth of a percent. And if you think about the total compensation paid to workers globally, which is maybe half of that, OpenAI capturing $100 billion would mean it's substituting for a very small fraction of human labor.

So I read the forecast as implying that OpenAI itself doesn't expect anything like a dramatic transformation of the economy by 2029. If they really believed they'd have systems by then that could do most remote work, or most cognitive tasks humans do, you'd expect revenue projections in the trillions, not in the hundreds of billions. Even if they only captured a small slice of the value they created, the numbers would be much bigger.

Now, you can push back on that in a few ways. One is that companies have reasons to be conservative in what they tell investors, or that revenue lags capabilities because adoption takes time. Businesses have to restructure workflows, there are regulatory issues, there's just inertia. I think that's a real effect, and historically general-purpose technologies took a long time to diffuse. But I don't think it fully explains the gap. If you had a genuine drop-in remote worker, the incentive to adopt would be enormous, and I'd expect diffusion to be much faster than with something like electricity.

The other thing I'd say is that this is roughly consistent with my own view. I don't expect AI to be automating a large share of the economy by the end of the decade. I think the capabilities that matter most for that, things like long-horizon agency, reliability over extended tasks, being able to operate in messy real-world contexts, and eventually physical manipulation through robotics, are harder than people in the industry often assume. Benchmarks keep falling, but the jump from impressive benchmark performance to economically substituting for a human worker across a whole job is large.

So my takeaway is that $100 billion by 2029 points to AI being a very significant industry, growing fast, but not yet a technology that's driving, say, a big acceleration in GDP growth. I do think that kind of acceleration is plausible eventually, maybe over the next couple of decades, but this forecast suggests even the most bullish lab doesn't expect it within the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says $100 billion would not imply a dramatic economic transformation or GDP growth acceleration by 2029, but it does not state that this revenue level is insufficient to create intense economic feedback loops driving AI progress.

r002.rationale: The response predicts limited economic automation by 2029, but does not identify a slowdown in AI progress as the most plausible outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that $100 billion by 2029 is actually not a very aggressive forecast if you take seriously the idea that AI is going to be transformative. It sounds like a big number, but you have to put it in context. The global economy is on the order of $100 trillion. So $100 billion is one tenth of one percent of world GDP. There are plenty of individual companies that already have revenue at that scale: Nvidia is past that, Microsoft and Google are well above it. So if OpenAI is just a very successful software company, you'd expect them to get there, and the forecast is basically consistent with AI being a big deal in the way the internet or cloud computing was a big deal.

What it doesn't look like, to me, is a forecast from a company that expects to be deploying something like a drop-in replacement for human workers in a few years. If you really thought you'd have systems in 2028 or 2029 that could do most remote work at the level of a competent professional, then $100 billion is a wild underestimate. The wage bill for the kind of work that could be automated is tens of trillions of dollars. Even capturing a small fraction of that would blow past $100 billion by an order of magnitude or more. So I read the number as implicitly encoding a view, maybe not a deliberate one, that progress over the next few years is going to look more like continued strong scaling of a useful product, rather than the kind of discontinuous economic takeoff that some people at these labs talk about publicly.

Now, there are caveats. One is that revenue lags capability. Even if you had very capable systems, diffusion through the economy takes time: firms need to restructure workflows, there are regulatory and trust issues, there are compute constraints on how much inference you can actually serve. So you could imagine a world where the models are much better than the revenue suggests. But I'd push back on that a bit, because I think if the systems were really that capable, you'd see it in the numbers faster than people expect. Businesses are pretty good at paying for things that clearly make them money.

The other caveat is that this is a forecast made for investors, and those tend to be shaped by what's credible to investors rather than by the forecaster's true median. If you told investors you expected $2 trillion in revenue by 2029, they would probably discount everything else you said. So there's some selection on what gets written down.

But overall, I'd say the forecast is consistent with my own view, which is that progress is going to be fast and economically significant, that AI revenue will grow at rates that would be remarkable for any other technology, maybe doubling every year or so, but that we're probably not going to see full automation of the economy within this decade. The $100 billion number is a world where the trends continue roughly as they have, and the compute scaleup keeps delivering, but where there's still a lot of work left to do on the things that currently keep these systems from being general-purpose workers: reliability, long-horizon agency, operating in messy real-world contexts. That's a world I put a lot of probability on.

r001.rationale: The response calls the forecast modest relative to transformative AI and discusses revenue growth, but does not state that it is insufficient to generate intense economic feedback loops driving AI progress.

r002.rationale: The response expects fast, economically significant progress and says trends will continue roughly as they have; it does not identify a slowdown by the end of the decade as the most plausible outcome.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about translating that revenue forecast directly into a forecast of AI capabilities. You can get to $100 billion in annual revenue through some combination of better models, more users, and deeper adoption of capabilities that already exist. Those imply quite different rates of technical progress.

But it does suggest that OpenAI expects demand to grow enormously, and that matters because revenue can finance further investment in compute and research. If the commercial returns materialize, it becomes easier to sustain the spending that drives progress.

The interesting question is what capabilities they’re assuming behind that number. If they expect AI to automate a large fraction of economically valuable work by 2029, $100 billion could actually look fairly modest. If they’re mostly expecting broader adoption of assistants, it’s an ambitious business forecast without necessarily being a prediction of radically more capable AI. So I’d treat it as evidence about their commercial expectations, but not as a precise timeline for something like AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says the forecast does not precisely predict capabilities or an AGI timeline, but it does not state that the revenue is insufficient to create intense economic feedback loops driving progress. It instead notes that revenue could finance further investment.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a slowdown by the end of the decade as the most plausible outcome.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty aggressive forecast commercially, but it’s much less clear what it implies about capabilities. You can imagine getting to $100 billion in revenue by making existing kinds of AI systems more reliable, cheaper, and more widely used. There are a lot of people and businesses that could pay for those services without the systems being able to automate entire jobs.

On the other hand, if you expect AI to become capable of doing a very large fraction of economically valuable work by 2029, $100 billion might actually seem quite small. So I wouldn’t read the forecast as a straightforward prediction of when we get AGI.

The connection to progress is that revenue can support further investment in training and deploying models. But revenue isn’t the same as profit, and it doesn’t tell you how much additional capability that investment will buy. I’d take it as evidence that OpenAI expects rapid commercialization, rather than as a precise forecast of the pace of AI progress.

r001.rationale: The response says revenue can support investment but does not state that the forecast is insufficient to generate intense economic feedback loops driving AI progress.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a slowdown by the end of the decade as the most plausible outcome; it says the revenue forecast is not a precise forecast of progress.
